title: Fractals in architecture: The visual interest, preference, and mood response to projected fractal light patterns in interior spaces
research_question: What effect do varying complexities of fractal light patterns projected on walls and floors of an interior space have on visual interest, visual preference, and mood responses?

participants.description: Study 1: 89 architecture/interior architecture students (51 females, 35 males, 3 declined to answer), age 18-29, from a human-factors course in the US. Study 2: 68 architecture/interior architecture students (27 male, 41 female), 78% 18-29, 18% 30-39, from an environmental control systems class in the US. Study 3: 32 participants (19 females, 12 males, 1 no answer), age 18-29 (26 participants), from the same pool as Study 1.
participants.recruitment: Recruited from human-factors and environmental control systems courses in an architecture department, via course learning management system and in-person.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Black and white fractal (D=1.1, 1.3, 1.5, 1.7) and non-fractal (Rectangular, Striped) patterns projected onto a white wall (8.0 × 8.0 feet) in a lecture hall using an overhead projector (Panasonic PT-DZ6700U, 1920x1200, 6000 Lumens). Patterns had 50% black-to-white ratio. White regions: 45 cd/m², black regions: 9 cd/m². Mean horizontal illuminance: 49 Lux. Vertical illuminance at projection wall: 23 Lux. Viewing distances varied from 5.1 m to 14 m.

Computer renderings of an office space with a side window, showing sunlight patterns (same 6 fractal and non-fractal patterns as Study 1) cast on the room's floor and opposite wall. Renderings generated using Autodesk Revit BIM software.

measures.instrument: Two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) procedure: 'Which light pattern is more visually interesting?'
5-point Likert-type scale: 'Does this light pattern make you feel [mood]? (Not at all - Extremely)'
Factor analysis of Calm/Peaceful (Relaxation) and Stimulated/Excited (Excitement)
Two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) procedure: 'Which light pattern is more visually preferred?'

findings.mechanism: The human visual system is adapted to efficiently process mid-complexity fractals prevalent in nature (fractal fluency theory).
findings.quote: Results showed that visual interest ratings peaked for mid-complexity fractals of D = 1.5, (Mean = 69.7%, SD = 18.27).
Further, the visual interest for fractals of D = 1.7 (Mean = 68.2%, SD = 27.3) and D = 1.3 (Mean = 65%, SD = 17.5) were not significantly different.

findings.mechanism: Non-fractal patterns lack the complexity and scaling properties that the human visual system is adapted to process efficiently.
findings.quote: Generally, the two non-fractal patterns, rectangular and the stripes, were significantly less visually interesting than all of the fractal patterns.
In addition, there was a significant difference (Z = 3.056, p < 0.01) between the visual interest ratings for the rectangular and striped light patterns.

findings.mechanism: Fractal patterns of higher complexity may induce greater stimulation.
findings.quote: Ratings for 'Excited' and 'Stimulated' feelings were highest at 2.25 and 2.96 for fractal patterns of D = 1.5 and D = 1.7, respectively (Fig. 7).

findings.mechanism: Fractal patterns of higher complexity may induce greater stimulation.
findings.quote: Ratings for 'Excited' and 'Stimulated' feelings were highest at 2.25 and 2.96 for fractal patterns of D = 1.5 and D = 1.7, respectively (Fig. 7).

findings.mechanism: Higher complexity may be less conducive to feelings of calm.
findings.quote: 'Calm' and 'Peaceful' ratings gradually dropped as the fractal dimension increased.

findings.mechanism: Higher complexity may be less conducive to feelings of peacefulness.
findings.quote: 'Calm' and 'Peaceful' ratings gradually dropped as the fractal dimension increased.

findings.mechanism: Fractal patterns, similar to nature, provide a balance of stimulation and relaxation, contributing to restorative experiences.
findings.quote: the fractal patterns maintained more balance between Relaxation and Excitement, as compared to D = 1.1 and non-fractal patterns.

findings.mechanism: Increased viewing distance in renderings may shift the peak preference to higher D values due to reduced perceived fine-scale detail.
findings.quote: The fractal light pattern with D = 1.7 was the most preferred (Mean = 70.2%, SD = 29.4), and was significantly more preferred than all other patterns.

findings.mechanism: Increased viewing distance in renderings may shift the peak preference to higher D values due to reduced perceived fine-scale detail.
findings.quote: The fractal with D = 1.5 received the second highest ratings for visual interest (Mean = 64.2%, SD = 19.3).
The rectangular pattern was significantly the least preferred light pattern (Mean = 15.8%, SD = 18.6).

findings.antecedent: non-fractal light patterns (Stripes) in renderings vs. fractal light patterns (D=1.1) in renderings
findings.mechanism: This finding contrasts with Study 1, possibly due to the medium (renderings) or perceived detail.
findings.quote: a contrasting finding was that the striped light pattern (Mean = 54.1, SD = 33.4) was found to be significantly more visually interesting than the low-complexity fractal with D = 1.1 (Mean = 38.3, SD = 21.6).

findings.mechanism: Mid-complexity fractals in renderings may still provide restorative benefits, though muted compared to direct projection.
findings.quote: The fractal light pattern with D = 1.5 provided the highest levels for Relaxation and excitement (Mean = 1.86 and 1.72, respectively).

findings.mechanism: Mid-complexity fractals in renderings may still provide stimulating benefits, though muted compared to direct projection.
findings.quote: The fractal light pattern with D = 1.5 provided the highest levels for Relaxation and excitement (Mean = 1.86 and 1.72, respectively).

findings.mechanism: Simple, non-fractal patterns are perceived as dull and less stimulating.
findings.quote: Similar to the results of Study 1, the rectangular light pattern resulted in an excitement level (Mean = 0.51) significantly lower than all of the other patterns.

findings.antecedent: medium of presentation (renderings vs. direct projection)
findings.mechanism: Renderings may be less experiential and thus elicit a muted emotional response compared to direct projection.
findings.quote: In comparison to the results of Study 1, mean excitement levels for all light patterns were notably lower.

findings.mechanism: Visual interest is highest for mid-complexity fractals, consistent with the fractal fluency theory.
findings.quote: main effect of Fractal Dimension F(3,84)=5.94, p=0.010

findings.antecedent: fractal dimension (D) x assessment type (visual interest vs. preference)
findings.mechanism: Visual interest and preference, while related, are distinct concepts influenced differently by fractal complexity.
findings.quote: interaction between Fractal Dimension and Assessment Type F(3,84)=6.96, p=0.001

findings.antecedent: viewing distance (front vs. back) x assessment type (visual interest vs. preference)
findings.mechanism: The type of assessment (interest vs. preference) may interact with viewing distance to influence responses.
findings.quote: interaction between Distance and Assessment Type F(1,28)=6.01, p=0.010

findings.mechanism: Participants may not have been able to resolve the finest details from any distance, negating the effect of distance on perceived complexity.
findings.quote: no significant difference in response choices related to seating distance from the screen (F(1,28)=0.025, p=0.875).

findings.mechanism: Visual interest peaks at mid-to-high complexity for projected patterns, possibly due to increased viewing distance.
findings.quote: Visual interest peaked D=1.5 (Mean=64.3, SD=22.3) and D=1.7 (Mean=65.1, SD=26.2).

findings.mechanism: Visual preference peaks at mid-to-high complexity for projected patterns, possibly due to increased viewing distance.
findings.quote: Visual preference peaked D=1.5 (Mean=64.3, SD=22.3) and D=1.7 (Mean=65.1, SD=26.2).

findings.mechanism: At higher D values, visual interest and preference may converge.
findings.quote: Visual interest and preference ratings were similar for D=1.5 and D=1.7.

findings.mechanism: At lower D values, visual interest and preference may diverge.
findings.quote: Visual interest and preference ratings were different for D=1.1 and D=1.3.

mechanisms: The human visual system is adapted to efficiently process mid-complexity fractals (fractal fluency theory), leading to positive perceptual and mood responses.

Increased viewing distance reduces the perceived fine-scale detail of fractal patterns, requiring higher fractal dimensions (D) to achieve the same perceived visual complexity and maintain visual interest/preference.
The medium of presentation (direct projection vs. renderings) influences the intensity of mood responses, with renderings eliciting more muted effects.

Figure-ground segregation: When patterns are projected on a wall, there is less separation between the pattern and the room, leading to higher attention and enhanced visual processing of the room itself.

Differences in light intensity and contrast between projected patterns and computer screen displays may affect the ability to resolve fine-scale details, influencing perceived complexity and preferred D values.
moderators: medium of presentation (direct projection vs. renderings)
assessment type (visual interest vs. visual preference)
implementation_implications: Utilizing medium to medium-high complexity fractal light patterns (D=1.5-1.7) in interior spaces can enhance occupants' visual interest and mood.

These findings have implications for the design of façade systems and shading systems, such as roller shades and perforated screens, to manipulate sunlight pattern geometry for visual interest and mood enhancement.
The use of fractal light patterns in interior spaces may elicit restorative and biophilic benefits similar to those of nature scenes.

limitations: The studies did not include a fractal pattern with D=1.9 due to concerns about participant fatigue and experiment duration.
The D increment between fractal patterns was 0.2, which might limit comparison to studies using different increments.
The use of renderings in Study 2 may have muted mood responses compared to direct physical projection.
The study did not fully explore the relationship between perceived complexity and scaling range, which could explain the shift in preferred D values.
The inability of participants to resolve the finest details from any distance might have masked the effect of viewing distance on D preference.
The studies were conducted in windowless rooms, and the presence of windows or daylight might introduce competing factors that influence visual interest, which was not assessed.
